key_insight: Jev was fast and inexpensive, but its performance was uneven: strong on PubMedQA, calibrated on MetaMedQA, and clearly weaker on harder diagnostic and case-based tasks.
clinical_relevance: Before any clinical use, a benchmarked answer-choice model like Jev needs task-specific validation because good calibration does not guarantee reliable diagnostic performance.
method: Evaluated Jev 1.13 on four medical benchmarks: MetaMedQA, PubMedQA, DiagnosisArena-MCQ, and NEJM Case Challenges.
Compared performance against GPT-6 Sol with and without medium reasoning.
Assessed top-1 accuracy, calibration, selective prediction, and recognition of unanswerable questions.
evidence_signal: Across 8,469 requests, Jev returned valid answers every time; accuracy ranged from 78.4% on PubMedQA to 59.8% on DiagnosisArena-MCQ, with median latency of 0.27-0.31 seconds and total cost of USD 0.08 for 2,823 items.
watch_item: Because Jev can only choose from predefined options, it may struggle with complex or out-of-distribution clinical reasoning and should not be deployed without task-specific validation.
paper_title: Jev in Medicine: A Benchmark Evaluation. Preliminary Results
